issues.description: Blocking read loop has no timeout; subprocess hang after first byte deadlocks parent forever
issues.detail: The original non-blocking loop bounded total wait via the outer `timeout` parameter passed to `select.poll().poll()`. Once the patch flips O_NONBLOCK off after a single 8192-byte chunk arrives, the inner `while True: os.read(fifo_fd, 8192)` has no timeout, no signal handling, and no process-exit check. If the writer subprocess writes one chunk, then stalls or hangs without closing the FIFO, the parent blocks indefinitely. The previous code explicitly handled this case via `check_process_exited(command_obj)`; that escape hatch is now removed. The invariant 'we make progress or we surface a failure within timeout' is violated.

issues.description: Loop invariant is not stated and the two-phase state machine is undocumented
issues.detail: The function now operates in two distinct phases (non-blocking poll-until-first-byte, then blocking drain-until-EOF), but no comment states the invariant tying them together, nor why the mode switch is safe at exactly that point. A reader has to reconstruct the POSIX argument from the commit message, which will not be present at the call site six months from now. The literate-programming-grade comment that motivates the patch belongs in the code, including a one-line statement of what is true at the top of each iteration and why the blocking read is guaranteed to terminate (writer-close implies drained pipe).

issues.description: fcntl mode switch is not restored and is not exception-safe
issues.detail: `fcntl.fcntl(fifo_fd, fcntl.F_SETFL, flags & ~os.O_NONBLOCK)` mutates kernel state on a file descriptor whose lifetime extends beyond this function. If `os.read` raises (e.g., EINTR, EIO) inside the blocking loop, the fd remains in blocking mode for any subsequent caller, and there is no try/finally to restore the original flags. For a utility named `read_from_fifo_when_ready` this is an action-at-a-distance side effect that violates the function's apparent contract.

issues.description: BlockingIOError path is now unreachable dead code
issues.detail: After the mode switch, `os.read` on a blocking fd will not raise BlockingIOError; before the mode switch, the only `os.read` call is followed by `if data: ... break` or the else branch, neither of which can produce BlockingIOError on the path that reaches the `except`. The `except BlockingIOError: pass` is therefore either dead or paper over a case the author has not analyzed. Either prove it cannot fire and delete it, or document the scenario that triggers it. Leaving an `except: pass` without an invariant is the anti-pattern the brief explicitly calls out.

issues.description: Outer poll/timeout becomes effectively one-shot, contradicting its name
issues.detail: The function still accepts a `timeout` argument used by `select.poll().poll(timeout)`, but it now only governs the wait for the first byte. After that, the timeout is silently irrelevant. Either rename the parameter to reflect 'time-to-first-byte timeout' or carry a deadline through the blocking phase (e.g., via `select` on the fd before each read, or `signal.alarm`). The current naming will mislead callers about worst-case latency.

issues.description: Complexity/throughput claim of the 8192 chunk size is unaudited under the new path
issues.detail: Total time is O(N/8192) syscalls where N is payload size; for the 86KB case in the bug report this is ~11 reads, which is fine. But once the function is committed to blocking mode, a larger buffer (e.g., 64KB) would cut syscall count materially with no downside, since latency-to-first-byte is no longer the constraint. Not load-bearing for correctness; flagging because the patch is the right moment to revisit, and because the constant should be a named symbol with a one-line justification rather than a bare literal repeated twice.

review.summary: UNDER-AUDITED with one likely P0. The diagnosis (kernel pipe buffers may hold data after subprocess exit; blocking read drains them per POSIX) is correct and the mode-switch idea is sound. The implementation, however, removes the only bound on total wait time: once any byte arrives, the function enters an unbounded blocking loop with no timeout, no process-exit check, and no signal handling, which trades an intermittent JSONDecodeError for an intermittent deadlock. Secondary issues are absence of a stated loop invariant for the two-phase state machine, a non-restored and non-exception-safe fcntl mutation on a fd whose lifetime escapes the function, and a now-unreachable BlockingIOError handler. Recommend: add a per-read timeout or `select` before each blocking read, restore O_NONBLOCK in a finally, and write the literate comment that explains why the blocking phase is guaranteed to terminate.
